current_example.problem: Use the extended Euclidean algorithm to compute the multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86.$
current_example.worked_solution:
First of all, notice that $\textrm{gcd}(15,86)=1.$ So, the multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86$ exists.

The multiplicative inverse of $15$ modulo $86$ is the number $x$ such that

$$
15\cdot x \equiv 1 \quad (\textrm{mod}\:86).
$$

To find the value of $x,$ we will use the extended Euclidean algorithm. First, we apply the forward reduction:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}86 & = & 15\cdot 5 & + & 11 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 15 & = & 11\cdot 1 & + & 4 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 11 & = & 4\cdot 2 & + & 3 \\  & ↙ &  & ↙ &  \\ 4 & = & 3\cdot 1 & + & 1\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Solving for the rightmost terms in the equations above, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}11 & =86-15\cdot 5 \\ 4 & =15-11 \\ 3 & =11-4\cdot 2 \\ 1 & =4-3.\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we back-substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4-3 \\  & =4-(11-4\cdot 2) \\  & =4\cdot 3-11 \\  & =(15-11)\cdot 3-11 \\  & =15\cdot 3-11\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 3-(86-15\cdot 5)\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 23-86\cdot 4 \\  & =15\cdot 23+86\cdot (-4)\end{aligned}
$$

We can write this result modulo $86,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}15\cdot 23+86\cdot (-4) & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,86) \\ 15\cdot 23 & ≡1 &  & (\text{mod}\,86)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $15\cdot 23\equiv 1 \: (\textrm{mod}\:86),$ which means that $15^{-1} \: \textrm{mod} \: 86=\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}23}.$
